sections.h2: Where do Taylor County property tax matters get handled?
sections.html:
Taylor County keeps its tax offices close together in Campbellsville. The sheriff, the Property Valuation Administration (PVA) and the county clerk all sit on North Court Street, so one trip can cover a payoff, an exemption form and a lien check.

The sheriff's page also points owners to an online portal where 2026 property tax information can be searched and paid. Pop-ups must be enabled in the browser for the portal to open.

sections.h2: What is Taylor County like for a home seller?
sections.html:
Taylor County was organized in 1848 and was the 100th of Kentucky's 120 counties. Settlers came from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maryland and North Carolina after the Revolution, and the county was named for Zachary Taylor. It covers 277 square miles, 266 of them land, and its outline is shaped like a heart. Locals claim the geographic center of Kentucky, a claim neighboring counties dispute. The Civil War skirmish known as the Battle of Tebbs Bend was fought here.

Campbellsville is the seat and only city, with communities such as Acton, Hobson, Mannsville and Saloma scattered around it. Marion, Casey, Adair, Green and LaRue counties border Taylor. The Green and Adair county lines also mark the Central time boundary, and the community of Black Gnat straddles it. Two public school systems serve the county: Campbellsville Independent and Taylor County Schools. About half the 2020 population, 49.1 percent, lived in an urban area, while Spencer, Todd and Trigg counties had no urban residents in that count.

Campbellsville University is the standout employer. A 2021 impact study released by the university counted 1,866 jobs it supports in Taylor County and put its main-campus economic impact at about $174.6 million. The Census Bureau's figures for businesses are consistent with a regional hub:

  • Retail sales in 2022 totaled $1.09 billion, about $41,299 per resident.
  • Health care and social assistance receipts reached $245.8 million.
  • Employer establishments numbered 631 in 2023, with 9,968 employees.

sections.h2: How does Taylor County housing compare in the Census numbers?
sections.html:
The population stands at 26,763 as of July 2025, up 2.8 percent from the 2020 base. The median owner-occupied home is valued at $174,200, and 68.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied. Renting is common: the 2020 census found 35.9 percent of occupied units rented, and the typical gross rent is $718.

Median household income is $60,456 across 10,260 households, and workers average a 22.7-minute commute. The Census Bureau counted just 9 building permits in 2025, a thin supply of new construction beside 11,247 housing units countywide.

sections.h2: When are Taylor County tax bills due and what are the penalties?
sections.html:
Kentucky's collection statute makes property taxes payable to the sheriff by December 31 of the assessment year, with the following stages applying to a regular schedule:

  • Paid in full by November 1 of the assessment year: a 2 percent discount.
  • November 2 to December 31: the face amount, with no discount and no penalty.
  • January: a 5 percent penalty on the unpaid tax.
  • February onward: a 10 percent penalty, plus the sheriff's add-on fee that the Department of Revenue shows on its delinquency worksheet.

A bill still open at the close of business on April 15 stops being a sheriff matter. The clerk's page puts it plainly: Taylor County bills become delinquent on April 15 each year.

sections.h2: What does the Taylor County clerk do with unpaid bills?
sections.html:
The clerk collects delinquent taxes with help from the county attorney, who writes to each owner. Two letters go out, and the delinquent list is advertised in the Central Kentucky News Journal. If bills remain open after all three notices, they are offered to third-party companies that can buy the bill and place a lien on the property. The clerk's page says bills are never sold to those companies before August, and the full list and sale date are posted on the clerk's website as the date nears.

The statewide numbers show how fast a small debt grows. In the Revenue Department's worked example, a $1,000 bill becomes a $1,254 certificate once the penalty, the sheriff's add-on and an assumed commission are counted. The certificate then picks up 1 percent interest a month plus a 10 percent clerk commission, and a 20 percent county attorney commission once the first notice is mailed. Paying inside five business days of the transfer avoids the attorney's fee.

sections.h2: How can I appeal a Taylor County assessment?
sections.html:
The PVA values most real property by comparing recent sales of similar homes and must inspect every parcel at least once in four years. You must meet with the PVA's office before you can appeal, and the PVA at Suite 6 can arrange the conference. The assessment roll is open to inspection for thirteen days from the first Monday of May, six days a week including Saturday. When you have had your conference, you file the appeal at the clerk's office by the end of the next workday.

A panel of local property owners hears the case 25 to 35 days after the roll closes. Bring facts: building characteristics, insurance values, construction costs, or listings of comparable property. The board denies an appeal that arrives without evidence. A representative who is paid for the work must be an attorney, accountant, real estate broker, certified appraiser or an employee of the owner, and needs written authorization.

Farm acreage is valued differently. Kentucky assesses farmland at its agricultural value rather than its market value. That can cut a bill sharply near cities and matters less in rural areas, where the two values sit closer together. Taxable personal property must be listed with the PVA by May 15 each year.

sections.h2: Who gets the homestead exemption in Taylor County?
sections.html: A homeowner who is 65 or older, or totally disabled under a federal or retirement-system program, can have $49,100 taken off the assessment for the 2025 and 2026 tax periods. Apply with Form 62A350 at the PVA before December 31. One exemption is allowed per household even when both spouses qualify, and a new owner has to apply again after a sale.

sections.h2: What should I do about taxes when selling a Taylor County house?
sections.html: Ask the sheriff for the exact payoff, then ask the clerk whether the parcel carries a certificate of delinquency from an earlier year. State law treats each year's tax as the personal debt of the January 1 owner, and a delinquent lien runs with the land for up to eleven years. If a third-party company holds the bill, the payoff goes to that company, not to the clerk.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Taylor County property taxes?
faqs.a: Pay the sheriff at 203 North Court Street, Suite 7 in Campbellsville, or use the online portal for 2026 payments. Phone (270) 465-4351 if you want to confirm the amount first.

faqs.q: When do Taylor County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: April 15 of the year after the assessment year. At that point unpaid bills move from the sheriff to the county clerk for collection.

faqs.q: Does Taylor County sell delinquent tax bills?
faqs.a: Yes, after three notices. The clerk says bills are not sold to third-party companies until August, and a purchaser's lien then attaches to the property.

faqs.q: How do I apply for the homestead exemption in Taylor County?
faqs.a: File Form 62A350 with the PVA office at (270) 465-5811 by December 31. You must be 65 or older, or totally disabled, and the home must be your residence on January 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Taylor County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes, because the tax is a lien that is paid from the sale. Get written payoff figures from the sheriff and the clerk so the closing agent can clear every year that is open.
